what_its_for: Lacosamide is a seizure medicine (also called an antiepileptic or anticonvulsant). It is used to treat partial-onset seizures in adults and children who are at least 1 month old. It may be used alone or together with other seizure medicines.
how_to_take: Take lacosamide exactly as your doctor tells you. You can take it with or without food. Swallow tablets whole — do not crush or chew them. If you are using the liquid (oral solution), use the measuring device provided with your medicine — do not use a household spoon. If you receive lacosamide as an IV infusion in a clinic or hospital, a healthcare professional will give it to you. Do not stop taking this medicine suddenly without talking to your doctor, as this can cause more seizures.
dosing: Your doctor will choose the right dose for you based on your weight, age, and how well it works for you. Most adults start on a low dose and the doctor slowly increases it over time. A common adult starting dose is 50 mg twice a day (morning and evening), and it may be increased up to 200–400 mg per day total. Always take your doses at the same times each day to keep a steady level of medicine in your body. Never change your dose on your own.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember — but only if it is still more than 6 hours before your next scheduled dose. If it is less than 6 hours until your next dose, skip the missed dose and just take your next dose at the regular time. Never take two doses at once to make up for a missed one.
storage: Store tablets and liquid at room temperature, between 68°F and 77°F (20°C to 25°C). Keep the bottle tightly closed. Keep away from heat, moisture, and direct light. Do not store in the bathroom. Throw away any unused oral solution 7 weeks after first opening the bottle. Keep all medicines out of reach of children and pets.
what_to_avoid: Avoid drinking alcohol while taking lacosamide — it can increase dizziness and make side effects worse. Be careful with activities that require you to be alert, such as driving, operating heavy machinery, or climbing, until you know how this medicine affects you, as it can cause dizziness, blurred vision, or coordination problems. Tell all your doctors and pharmacist about every medicine, vitamin, supplement, or herbal product you take, as some medicines can interact with lacosamide.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or go to the emergency room if you experience: new or worsening depression, thoughts of suicide or self-harm, unusual changes in mood or behavior, chest pain, slow or irregular heartbeat, fainting or feeling lightheaded, severe skin rash or blistering, swollen glands, fever, or signs of an allergic reaction (rash, swelling of face or throat, trouble breathing). Also contact your doctor if your seizures get worse or occur more often, or if you develop memory problems or confusion.
when_it_works: Lacosamide starts working relatively quickly — within a few days of reaching the right dose. However, it may take several weeks to find the best dose that controls your seizures with the fewest side effects. Do not stop taking it just because you feel better or because seizures have stopped. Keep taking it as prescribed.
special_populations: Pregnant women: Talk to your doctor before taking lacosamide if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding. Seizure medicines can affect pregnancy, but stopping them can also be dangerous. Enroll in the North American Antiepileptic Drug (NAAED) Pregnancy Registry by calling 1-888-233-2334. Breastfeeding: It is not known if lacosamide passes into breast milk — discuss the risks and benefits with your doctor. Elderly patients (over 65): Older adults may be more sensitive to side effects like dizziness and falls — use extra caution. Kidney or liver problems: Your doctor may need to give you a lower dose if you have moderate to severe kidney or liver disease. Children: Lacosamide can be used in children as young as 1 month old — the dose will be based on the child's weight.
